articles.title: Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse Is Up for Preorder
articles.summary: Everything you need to know to preorder Castlevania: Belmont's Curse, the first brand-new side-scrolling Castlevania game since 2008.
articles.body:
Castlevania? Now that's a name I've not heard in a long time. After years of making almost no video games at all, Konami has decided to get back into the fray with a handful of new game announcements in beloved franchises. Among the upcoming releases is Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse, a new side-scrolling entry in the long-dormant action-horror series.

Belmont’s Curse is set to release Thursday, October 15 for PS5, Nintendo Switch, Xbox, and PC. It’s already available to preorder for $39.99 ( see it on Amazon ). Below, we dive into what this game is and where you can place your preorder. Let’s get to it.

Castlevania: Belmont's Curse (PS5, Xbox, Switch)

Unlike many games these days, only one edition is available, so the standard version is all you get. That’s cool though, because it comes with the game, and that’s the most important component of any game release, if you ask me.

The digital editions aren’t even available at the time of this writing, so it’s possible a digital deluxe edition goes up for preorder when those go live. I’ll update the article when it becomes available on digital storefronts.

As yet, no preorder bonuses have been announced. If any become available in the future (which does happen from time to time), this is where you’ll find them.

Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse is the first brand-new side-scrolling Castlevania game since 2013’s Castlevania: Lords of Shadow – Mirror of Fate came out on the Nintendo 3DS. That’s 13 years! It’s published by Konami, but it’s being developed by Evil Empire, the company behind The Rogue Prince of Persia and several Dead Cells DLCs, including Dead Cells: Return to Castlevania . So they know their way around a side-scrolling action game. Motion Twin, the main developer of Dead Cells, is also on board in an advisory role.

Belmont’s Curse takes place in 1499 Paris, which is in the midst of a monster invasion. That puts it 23 years after the events of the NES game Castlevania III: Dracula’s Curse . It’s not 100% clear if this is a “metroidvania” or “search action” game in the vein of Castlevania: Symphony of the Night and the GBA and Nintendo DS installments of the early 2000s.

In terms of gameplay, it looks like you do plenty of jumping on platforms, swinging from rings, and whipping on enemies. Bosses can tower over you. Environmental hazards like saw blades are strewn about. You have access to additional weapons and abilities like a flame spell and a cross you can throw like a boomerang. It looks like fun. Watch the trailer above to see for yourself.

Chris Reed is a commerce editor and deals expert for IGN. He also runs IGN's board game and LEGO coverage. You can follow him on Bluesky .

articles.title: So you want to buy a handheld gaming PC
articles.summary: The Verge’s handheld gaming PC buying guide is here. It may be a bad time to buy, but we won’t talk you out of it.
articles.body: Gaming handhelds are amazing. They make it so much easier to fit all kinds of games into my day. Sadly, they’re less affordable than they’ve ever been — due to an unprecedented, AI-fueled shortage of memory chips, an unforced oil crisis, rampant inflation, fallout from tariffs, and more. But that’s not going to stop you. You’ve decided now’s the time to buy one, before the next shoe drops. I won’t talk you out of it! I genuinely don’t know when or if prices might come back down. So instead of telling you to hold off, I’ll try to help you navigate this “new normal” I keep hearing so much about. We’ll do this four ways: * First, if you just want me to tell you what to buy and be done with it, grab an Xbox Ally X if it’s still $999 by the time you read these words. It’s the handheld I’d buy for myself if I were buying today. It’s the only top-tier handheld that hasn’t hiked its price, and it has a good mix of performance, comfort, and battery life. * Second, let’s talk bargains. There are a few refurbished and open-box handhelds worth nabbing on closeout — if you can find them at all. * Third, I’ll ask you some questions. Assuming you’re buying new, are you looking for the most powerful handheld? The one with the longest battery life? The most affordable? The best screen? The easiest to pick up and play? Because all of those are different handhelds, and none are the Xbox Ally X. Continue reading to find out which is which. * Fourth, I’ll list every other handheld PC you’re likely to find when you shop around, and why you should probably skip them. I want you to know whether that seemingly good closeout deal is actually worth your money. But before I go down the list, let’s talk Windows and Linux. While I’ve dinged many of the handhelds I’ve reviewed for The Verge for Windows woes, that’s not as big a deal today — because you can install Bazzite or even SteamOS on many of them for a better pick-up-and-play experience. The same exact handheld is often more stable and performant with Linux, and you often get instant sleep and resume that’s hit or miss on the operating system it shipped with. It’s still true that many competitive online multiplayer games don’t work on Linux because of anti-cheat fears, though others do. It’s also true that Windows has gotten better at sleep and resume with certain handhelds like the Xbox Ally X. But it’s a misconception that Linux can’t play as many games as Windows. The reality is that Linux can play more — decades of Windows games work better on Linux thanks to Proton patches and community profiles that translate old mouse and keyboard controls to your gamepad. Ready? Let’s go down each list, from least to most expensive. Open box and refurb bargains Refurbished Valve Steam Deck LCD (typically $279–$359) If you ever see it in stock, do not hesitate: Buy a refurbished Steam Deck LCD. Valve discontinued the original in December 2025, but Valve refurbs are now the best deal in town. The Steam Deck OLED meaningfully improved on the LCD model in many ways, but it is absolutely not worth $400 more than a certified refurbished LCD model. Reddit is flooded with examples of Valve’s excellent customer support, so I wouldn’t be worried about getting a lemon, and the Steam Deck LCD is one of the easier handhelds to pick up and play thanks to preloaded SteamOS and well-placed controls. It has enough performance for games as intensive as Elden Ring, but expect to play higher-end titles at low settings, with lots of upscaling, for less than two hours on battery. Light fare can last longer. [Image: The original Asus ROG Ally. Open-box Asus ROG Ally Z1 Extreme (typically $500–$550) At $500, if you’re willing to install Bazzite, and if you don’t play far from a cord, I can genuinely recommend the ROG Ally Z1E in today’s economy. It’s one of the weaker devices to carry that chip, with one of the smallest batteries at 40 watt-hours, but it’s also got the same kind of smooth (if not colorful) 7-inch 120Hz VRR screen you’ll find in the Xbox Ally X. When plugged into the wall, or in short sessions on battery, its turbo mode gives you Steam Deck-beating performance. [Image: The original Lenovo Legion Go might be a good deal at the right price. Open-box Lenovo Legion Go (sometimes $600 open box, normally $850) The original Legion Go is an acquired taste I’m never going to acquire: big, bulky, with extra buttons weirdly squishing under my hands when I grip. The battery’s only a little bigger than in the original ROG Ally, it doesn’t have a variable refresh rate screen, and the 2560 x 1600 resolution is far more than the chip can power in modern games. (Lightweight stuff can look good.) But Bazzite works great, and there’s a big 8.8-inch screen for those who need it, detachable controllers with a mouse mode, and a built-in kickstand; you can use it as a tablet in a pinch. I’d pick a Steam Deck over it any day, but the Z1 Extreme’s turbo mode makes it far faster for short sessions or plugged into the wall. Twin USB4 ports, too. And you can add the Legion Go 2’s more ergonomic controllers for roughly $100. (Don’t forget you need left and right ones.) As a $600 open-box deal, it’s worth it. But I wouldn’t pay much more. [Image: The Windows version of the Legion Go S is white. Closeout Lenovo Legion Go S Z2 Go with Windows ($550 closeout, normally $1,600) Almost the polar opposite of the original Legion Go, with no detachable controls, a smooth variable refresh rate screen at a more sensible 1920 x 1200 resolution, comfortable grips — and a much slower AMD Z2 Go chip that couldn’t meaningfully compete with the Steam Deck in my Windows tests. At $550 closeout like we saw the other day, sure, put Bazzite on it. It should slightly beat the Steam Deck in performance using its turbo modes after that. Please don’t pay much more. Also please don’t expect its tiny trackpad to be useful. Refurbished Valve Steam Deck OLED 512GB ($629) I hate to admit it, but if you ever see a refurbished Steam Deck OLED for $629, you might want to spend the money. Yes, Valve is charging $190 more for the refurb model than it did before RAMageddon, but it’s still a discount of $160 compared to what a Deck OLED costs brand-new today and “only” $80 more than what a new one cost before the price hikes. As I’ll explain a few paragraphs below, the Deck OLED is still one of the best handhelds you can buy. So those are the closeouts. Here’s what I’d suggest if you’re buying brand-new: [Image: The Asus Xbox Ally. The most affordable handheld you can actually find: Asus Xbox Ally ($600 MSRP, sometimes $500 on sale) When the Steam Deck OLED could be had for $549, there was no way I’d have ever recommended a vanilla white Xbox Ally instead. Now that the Deck starts at $789, I have to reconsider. The Xbox Ally has very comfortable prong-shaped grips and effectively the same chip as the Steam Deck, only you can crank it up to 20 watts instead of 15 watts for more power, you get a smoother 120Hz VRR screen, and it has a slightly larger battery. I’ve never been able to get the Windows version to sleep reliably — I retested this month — and the screen feels cramped and dull by comparison. But Bazzite fixes sleep and performance, making it more than a match for the Deck. The build feels a little cheap (I broke the top off an analog stick and had to superglue it back on), and it’s nowhere near as powerful as any handheld with a Z1 Extreme or better. The Xbox Ally X and MSI Claw 8 have larger batteries, too, and you don’t get the Steam Deck’s twin touchpads, four back buttons, and community controller profiles. But I’d buy it if I didn’t want to spend more than $600. [Image: The Steam Deck OLED. The easiest to pick up and play: Steam Deck OLED ($789 for 512GB, $949 for 1TB, $629 or $759 refurbished) When it comes to portable PC gaming, nothing “just works” like a Steam Deck OLED. You power it on, you scan a QR code to connect your Steam account, you download, you play, you get a solid two to eight hours of battery life on a fantastic screen without having to think about what performance mode to put your handheld in. The controls are infinitely customizable in ways the competition hasn’t even tried to match, and you can just browse community controller profiles instead of needing to roll your own. At $789, it’s a way harder sell than at $549, because if your budget stretches to $1,000, the Xbox Ally X’s performance and battery life are much better — and you can put Bazzite or SteamOS on that one, too. But I’d still buy a refurb Steam Deck OLED at $629, and I could see some paying $789 for its ease of use and unprecedented support: No company ships updates like Valve ships updates, regularly making the Deck better. [Image: The Xbox Ally X. The handheld I’d buy for myself: Xbox Ally X ($999) Like the Steam Deck, the Xbox Ally X originally shipped half-baked. Now, it’s suddenly the best deal in handheld gaming. While the 7-inch IPS screen feels a little claustrophobic and muted compared to 8-inch rivals, it’s now the most powerful handheld under $1,000 with its Z2 Extreme chip, one of the longest-lived with an 80 watt-hour battery, and (IMO) the most comfortable to hold with its huge prong grips. It’s also the best-supported outside of Valve’s Steam Deck; Asus and Microsoft keep shipping a flurry of updates. I can finally trust the Xbox Ally X to sleep and wake reliably, picking up my game right where I left off, and I can control the virtual keyboard by joystick instead of smudging a touchscreen. I can now tap the triggers to scroll the long clickwrap agreements that pop up before some games, too. Just know it’s not much more powerful than a Z1 Extreme or Z2 handheld, and the controls leave a few things to be desired. There’s no touchpad (and the joystick mouse mode is still finicky to enable), the ABXY buttons are very clacky, my triggers developed a noisy squeak, and I hate accidentally pressing the Library button thinking it’s Start and getting yanked out of a game. A future Ally fixes lots of these things, but it’ll be pricey. [Image: The MSI Claw 8 AI Plus. The longest battery life: MSI Claw 8 AI Plus* ($1,300, often $1,120 on sale) Frankly, I’m astonished how good the MSI Claw 8 can be. It’s got a bigger, better screen than the Xbox Ally X, and I find its Intel chip faster in the games I want to play — it gives me a smoother experience in 007: First Light and Clair Obscur: Expedition 33. And it lasts very slightly longer on the same capacity (80 watt-hour) battery, the longest I’ve tested so far. There are only four reasons it’s not the one I’d buy for myself. The scalloped grips aren’t as comfortable, the controls aren’t as customizable (and gyro doesn’t work as well), MSI just isn’t offering the same level of support (I’ve had to manually download drivers several times, for example), and it now costs a good bit more. I’d pick it if it were $900. *The newer EX version of the Claw 8 will come out this month with even better life, performance, and comfort, it seems — but it could cost much more. Read my preview. [Image: The Legion Go 2 in its mouse mode. The best screen: Legion Go 2 Z2 ($1,500) If your eyes are the priority, the Legion Go 2 has the best handheld screen money can buy today — not only is it the rare handheld with an OLED panel, and the inky blacks and gorgeous colors that can afford, it’s an HDR panel with 500-nit brightness and 1,000 nit peaks, plus variable refresh rate that goes all the way down to 30Hz and up to 144Hz for smoother gameplay. It’s a joy in person. The grips are far more comfortable than the original Legion Go, you still get the unique kickstand and detachable gamepads with optical mouse mode, the controls are competent, it has top and bottom USB-C ports, and the 74-watt-hour battery’s only a little smaller than other flagships. The things holding back the Legion Go 2 at launch were a high price and Windows. And while the price has gone up, the Z2 variant’s price hike isn’t quite as ridiculous as that of the Z2 Extreme. And the Z2 Legion Go 2 is pretty close to the Z2 Extreme version in performance — you should watch ETA Prime’s whole comparison video to see just how close. As for Windows, Bazzite seems to work well on my review unit of the Z2 Extreme model, though the gyro and some of Lenovo’s unique buttons can be a chore to configure there. [Image: The GPD Win 5. The most powerful: GPD Win 5 or OneXPlayer Apex (roughly $2,500 and up) I can’t afford a $2,500 handheld, but for those who want the ultimate in performance, AMD’s Strix Halo is the most powerful chip that fits between two hands. When I tested the GPD Win 5, it felt like a portable PS5, comfortably playing intensive games at 1080p resolution with ultra levels of detail. But beyond price, you should consider just how “portable” the Win 5 and the rival OneXPlayer Apex truly are: To cram in that power, they rely on either bulky external battery backpacks that won’t last an hour at full power, or a big power cord plugged into the wall. I also haven’t been offered full review units yet, so I don’t know whether GPD or OneXPlayer have nailed other fundamentals or are offering proper support. Proceed with caution. What if you’re not finding any of those handhelds? Be careful before you buy these alternatives instead: The handhelds you probably shouldn’t pay for Open-box Asus ROG Ally Z1 (typically $380–$450) Don’t be fooled: The Asus ROG Ally with a weaker AMD Z1 chip may look identical to the one with the Z1 Extreme, but this one’s less capable than a Steam Deck and less efficient last I checked. With one of the smallest batteries in a handheld (40 watt-hour, tied with the Steam Deck LCD) it’ll die quick, and it’s not as potent plugged in as the Z1E version. Unless you can find it for under $250 like ETA Prime did, leave it be. MSI Claw 7 ($650–$750) Somehow, Target still has stock of the original MSI Claw for $100 less than its original asking price, while Best Buy still has it at MSRP. Here is what I wrote in 2024: * “No one should buy an MSI Claw.” * “[T]he $750 MSI Claw feels like an inferior clone of the Asus ROG Ally.” * “The less expensive Steam Deck OLED all but completely wiped the floor with the MSI Claw in power and performance.” I hear Bazzite doesn’t fix this one, either. Just skip it. [Image: The Legion Go S with SteamOS isn’t bad with a Z1 Extreme, but neither it nor the Z2 Go version is worth current prices. Lenovo Legion Go S Z2 Go with SteamOS ($990) Another case of “don’t get fooled.” The Legion Go S with AMD’s Z2 Go is far weaker than the version with the older Z1 Extreme processor — or any other Z1 Extreme handheld. It can have a slight performance and battery advantage over the Steam Deck in more intensive games, but falls behind on battery in less demanding ones. Nice large smooth variable refresh rate screen, comfy grips, comes with SteamOS, but it wasn’t a good pick even when it cost $50 more than a Steam Deck OLED — now that it costs $200 more, forget about it. Ayaneo 3 ($1,183) I have never been able to recommend an Ayaneo handheld PC, because the company tends to ship them before they’re ready and quickly move on to the next thing. As exciting as it sounded, the Ayaneo 3 seems no different; I never got its awesome-sounding swappable controls to stay connected reliably, and the company didn’t have a solution for me. $900 for an fancy OLED handheld sounded enticing in 2025, but I wouldn’t recommend my experience at $400, let alone the $1,183 asking price now. MSI Claw A8 ($1,300, often $1,200 on sale) I haven’t used this one myself, but it costs substantially more than an Xbox Ally X for basically the same internals. Even used ones will cost you nearly $1,000. Bigger grips and screen, though. GPD Win Mini 2025 ($1,317) Haven’t used this one either, and I’m intrigued by the idea of a tiny handheld cyberdeck after my good experiences with the GPD Win Max 2 below. It’s got a 1080p VRR screen that should be better for gaming than the Win Max 2. But it also shot up in price from roughly $900 to over $1,300, and its Ryzen 7 8840U laptop chip will chew right through the small 44Wh battery in more than light-lift games. [Image: The GPD Win Max 2 is a surprisingly good tiny laptop, but an iffy handheld. GPD Win Max 2 ($1,494) The Win Max 2 is not a comfortable gaming experience, with weird grip and a fixed 60Hz 1600p screen, and the nearly $1,500 price tag hurts for something that cost $1,000 last year. But do you want maybe the tiniest laptop to ever have a keyboard this excellent, one that can double as an awkward gaming handheld in a pinch? I wouldn’t pay for it, but I will continue to hope a future version adds the bigger battery, VRR, vibration dampening, better mousing, and better webcam it needs. Lenovo Legion Go S Z1 Extreme with SteamOS ($1,580) or Windows ($1,680) $1,600 for a handheld with less performance and smaller battery than the Xbox Ally X and MSI Claw 8? Get outta here. It’s a legitimately good handheld, but even back when it cost $830 I’d have picked a Steam Deck instead. Now it costs nearly double — even more than the Legion Go 2 with a far better screen. Abxylute 3D One ($1,899) This giant honking 11-inch rebranded Tencent handheld theoretically has the same Intel guts as the MSI Claw 8 AI Plus, but it certainly doesn’t feel that way. The autostereoscopic 3D screen is terrible for gaming in my tests. It’s not very smooth even at its fixed 60Hz refresh rate, and gets ridiculously choppy in 3D mode without even providing a convincing 3D effect, even in 3D native games like Trine 2. I saw all kinds of crosstalk that better 3D screens cracked ages ago. I’d rather play Nintendo 3DS. Lenovo Legion Go 2 Z2 Extreme ($2,000–$2,350) Pretty much identical to the Legion Go Z2, save you’re paying $425 more for twice the RAM (32GB instead of 16GB) and slightly better battery life due to the more efficient chip. I wouldn’t.

articles.title: ‘Enough Games Have Been Cancelled and Shut Down. That Betrayal Has Ramifications’ – Is It the Beginning of the End for Live-Service Games?
articles.summary: Live-service dominates global playtime, but can it survive cancelled projects, dwindling players, and a market in decline? Or is this the beginning of the end for forever games?
articles.body:
Not too long ago, it felt like there was no escape from live-service games. Bethesda’s unveiling of Fallout 76 in 2018 felt like an ominous bellwether – was every iconic franchise now fated to transform into a forever game? Was ever-evolving multiplayer with seasonal content updates the way forward for our favourite RPGs and shooters?

Fast forward eight years and the landscape is looking very different. Major gaming publishers are cancelling live-service games left, right and centre, while many newcomers arrive on the scene only to pack up their bags and disappear within a few short months.

Some will, understandably, celebrate the apparent downturn of the live-service model. Others, meanwhile, will see this as cause for concern. The battle pass era has been a veritable financial feast for the video games industry’s revenue growth – if it disappears, does that profitable growth disappear along with it? For some, the problem is not the disappearance of “forever games”, but the reasons why the sector is contracting. And another group will even challenge the assertion that live-service is even disappearing at all.

Above all else, one thing is clear: there’s change on the horizon.

By the end of January this year, 15 of the 19 major new live-service games launched in 2025 had lost over 80% of their initial playerbase . Among them were big, recognisable, popular names, including Persona 5: The Phantom X, Runescape: Dragonwilds and Dune: Awakening. Leveraging known, beloved IP is no longer a surefire ticket to success, something Sega learned this year following weak performance of its free-to-play push, including the likes of mobile battle royale Sonic Rumble Party. This significant stall lead to Sega cancelling its mysterious 'Super Game'.

PlayStation has found itself in a similar situation. According to a recent Bloomberg report , the company has either halted or outright cancelled the development of over a dozen live-service games over the last decade. Many of these were linked to marquee IP like Spider-Man and God of War. Most recently, the controversial Horizon Hunters Gathering has been rebooted , with the aim of essentially ‘unmaking’ the live-service aspects and turning it into a traditional co-op game. This determination to make live-service work for Horizon means a new entry in the series’ core single-player series is reportedly still years away from release . It’s a similar story for gaming stalwart Naughty Dog, whose years spent on the ill-fated The Last of Us Online meant progress on its next major cinematic narrative game, Intergalactic: The Heretic Prophet, was slowed. TLOU Online was ultimately cancelled to prevent Naughty Dog transforming into a live-service studio, and the majority of that game’s developers moved over onto Intergalactic to allow for full-scale production .

It’s not just live-service newcomers that’re suffering, though; even the heavyweights are beginning to feel the squeeze. Newzoo’s latest gaming report showed a 27% decline in the battle royale sub-genre, with live-service heavyweights Fortnite and Apex Legends both suffering a drop in playtime growth of almost a quarter. Despite Marvel Rivals’ immense success, many of the top shooters also saw a drop-off of at least 15%, including Overwatch, Call of Duty, and Valorant. An even broader overview of the market reveals that the free-to-play model itself is in decline, with playtime on PC down 8%, PlayStation down 4% and Xbox down 11% in 2025 compared to 2024. It’s a small drop, but if it’s the start of a larger trend, the live-service model may be beginning to flatline.

So why the downturn? Ex-BioWare executive producer Mark Darrah, who helped guide the ill-fated Anthem to the finish line, thinks people may be finally realizing the gold rush is over. “I think there’s a glimmer of understanding that if you're making a looter shooter and it’ll be a ‘decent’ looter shooter, that’s not enough anymore,” he says.

The original director of MMORPG pioneer Ultima Online, Starr Long, notes that it’s difficult to hook players into the classic live-service play cycle if they don’t trust that the game will even be online next month. “Enough games have been cancelled and shut down, so at this point people have a trust issue,” he says. “Players are asking ‘Why should I commit myself?’ That betrayal has long-term ramifications.”

For publishers, part of the allure of live-service games are the measurable metrics. Darrah notes that publishers can predict a player’s individual financial input into live-service games based on many minute actions. What someone did on their first day can inform the company of that person’s playstyle and, consequently, how much money they may be willing to part with. But if people are logging off your game and not coming back – or not even picking it up in the first place – that number is a big, fat zero.

But the explanation may be far simpler: perhaps the live-service cycle is simply just ending. That’s how Kat Osman, team director at British video games communication agency Lick PR, sees it: “There was a time when it felt like the focus was entirely on FPS games, a time when dance and music-based games were popular – we’ve all got those dusty peripherals hidden away in cupboards.” She doesn’t believe the live-service model will ever fade away – Just Dance still releases a new game year-on-year, after all – but thinks the format’s shiny allure has finally faded.

But what is the next cycle, if not more live-service? The answer may be the indie game marketplace, which has exploded in such a way that it makes the previous indie boom look quaint. R.E.P.O., Peak and Schedule I sold over 40 million copies in 2025. This year’s mega-hit Meccha Chameleon has sold 20 million copies since June 2026 and is close to cracking the 50 best-selling games of all time.

“I think the space between triple-As and indies is actually smaller than it used to be,” says Osman. “The success of these heavy hitting indies means developers don’t always need a publisher now.”

The indie game industry accounted for $4.5 billion last year, and 25% of Steam’s $17.7 billion revenue . It’s only expected to expand; games analytics agency Mordor Intelligence predicts the market will grow to $10.8 billion by 2031 . However, this is only part of the picture; How To Market A Game’s 2025 study showed that of 20,282 games released, only 608 achieved a significant success benchmark. That’s just 2.99%. And, like triple-A studios, indie development teams have been subject to significant restructuring due to the wider state of the industry, with a third of indie developers reporting layoffs in the 2026 GDC State of Gaming report.

One thing is clear when viewing this picture as a whole: while the ability for indies to succeed on a similar level to triple-A titles feels more tangible than ever, the “double-A” space – those smaller budget games made by more traditionally-structured studios – feels more empty than ever. But perhaps that space is where the industry’s next big thing will be born.

If you’ve been keeping a close eye on the industry, you’ll have noticed that there’s a silver lining to the market over-indexing on live-service games and suffering the consequences. Several veteran triple-A developers have struck out on their own to create something brand-new. There’s Black Pony Immersive , formed of many former Arkane Austin developers and headed by Harvey Smith and Ben Horne; Hundred Star Games led by Rocksteady co-founders Sefton Hill and Jamie Walker; Studio Reset comprised of former BioWare, Inflexion Games, and Timbre Games staff, plus many more. One thing connects all of these new studios: they’re all founded by staff who once worked on critically-acclaimed single-player games, were pushed into live-service projects by their publishers, and are now trying to return the genres that they cut their teeth on. Should these games all prove successful, the next “cycle” may well be a series of double-A single-player projects that take us back to a time before daily challenges and battle passes.

But that potential double-A renaissance doesn’t need to totally reject its live-service past. There’s room for ever-evolving multiplayer projects at this scale, too, and that’s exactly what former Overwatch lead director Jeff Kaplan is working on. After a 19-year-long stint at Blizzard, Kaplan set up a new studio, Kintsugiyama, alongside his former colleague, Overwatch associate tech director Tim Ford. Their first game, The Legend of California is a multiplayer open world game set in the Californian gold rush of the 1800s. It’s a difficult game, inspired by Elden Ring’s interesting challenges, and adapts key features from some of the more prominent live-service games of the past decade, including procedurally generated maps that reset each month in a nod to Kaplan’s love of Rust.

The team’s mission statement is simple: get back to the open-world roots Kaplan put down during his days working on World of Warcraft. But this open world will look very different to Azeroth. Part survival crafter, part first-person-shooter, part action-RPG, The Legend of California hopes to be a home for a community of players who can shape its future. There is no clear roadmap – quite what it will look like in one, five, or even 10 years time will be informed by the playerbase. As with the entire history of live-service games, from the MMOs of the early 2000s to the battle royale behemoths of today, the future of the format – even at a much smaller scale than the triple-A beasts that have defined the past decade – will rely on a strong, healthy relationship between players and developers. And so Kaplan and his 30-person team at Kintsugiyama are determined to work with their players to create something satisfying, because, in his own words: “This environment is succeed or we don’t get to exist anymore.”

Regardless of what the next cycle proves to be, there’s reason to be optimistic that the next five years will see the industry move past the ‘dark times’ of publishers trying in vain to make the next Fortnite.

“I am a believer that from bad, some good can come, and from some tough times, the industry will once again flourish”, says Osman.

The incredible success of brand-new titles from first-time developers is seen by Darrah as a positive sign that things will improve. “What gives me hope is games like Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, where it feels like they’re answering the question of: ‘What if we take a $200 million budget and make four $50 million games?’” he says, noting developer Sandfall Interactive’s willingness to re-use sets and recycle assets from pre-existing kits to create something new as something that separates it from modern triple-A studios.

Kaplan feels that the pieces are slowly aligning for a reinvigoration of the industry, buoyed by these newly created studios born during a pressurized ‘succeed or die’ era. “You’re going to see extreme innovation,” he says. “You’ll see some mega hits come out of indie, and you’ll see some knock it out of the park moments with triple-A. It’s going to take a while for the reset to happen, but when the right things align, we’ll absolutely see the return of blockbuster triple-A-level games again.”

As I outlined at the start of this article, live-service is starting to dip. And if that dip is the beginning of the end, is this the start of a catastrophic crash? So much money has been pumped into live-service, can failure really be a good thing for the industry? But instead of asking whether or not the video games industry can continue without live-service games, perhaps the better question we should be asking is: can video games heal from what live-service has inflicted upon it? When the industry crashed in 1983, with revenue falling from $3.2 billion to just $100 million, an over-saturation of weak-quality, under-developed and derivative games eroded players’ trust and lacerated the market. It didn’t end the industry, but it did scar it. Some may say the live-service model has left its own scar on the modern industry. But the influx of new independent studios could be a sign that the wound is closing, the scar slowly healing. If nothing else, it appears there are investors confident enough to fund games that don’t chase the live-service trend.

The next question, then, is will the industry remember how we got the scar in the first place? And will players embrace these new independent studios in the way they did live-service? In an age when fresh new ideas made on a micro-budget can dominate Steam, where new players have been raised on a diet of Roblox experiments, it really does feel like the future of games is anything but the rules established by the live-service giants.

Sab Astley is a freelance writer who has written for IGN, Polygon, TotalFilm, Rolling Stone, Radio Times, and Metro UK.

articles.title: 10 Best LEGO Sets in 2026
articles.summary: Of all the many LEGO sets on the market, from a variety of price points, these are our picks for the best of the bunch.
articles.body:
There are hundreds of LEGO sets out there, but any LEGO fan – even a dedicated one – will build a miniscule fraction of them. Display space is one reason. Price is another. And for the amount of money you spend, the final build had better reflect the expense and effort that went into it.

We went through all the current LEGO builds available, and we put together a "greatest hits" list. The LEGO designers set a high goal and over delivered in each of these instances.

Here are the Best LEGO Sets in 2026, as of October 2026 – the models that look phenomenal and are equally fun to build.

TL;DR – These Are the Best LEGO Sets in 2026

LEGO Jurassic World Dinosaur Fossils: Tyrannosaurus rex

One of the best LEGO sets of the past five years, this classic Mississippi steamboat is an expert set for an expert builder. Every brick – every rod and pin – has a purpose, and when you push the River Steamboat along, the paddle wheel turns along with it. We built and reviewed this set for its launch and were continually impressed by its fastidious attention to detail.

Ambitious to the extreme, as we can attest having built it , this scaled-down replica of the famed, doomed RMS Titanic is nearly 4-and-a-half feet long. You build in three parts – the fore, middle, and aft of the ship. And if you examine its interior, you can see the piston steam engine that attaches to the propeller, the famed grand staircase, and the ornate lounges that made Titanic the "ship of dreams."

Big, colorful, and bold, this Optimus Prime set can actually transform from an Autobot into a more inconspicuous semi-truck. Both versions of the build look equally good, and the transformation process does not 'cheat'; you bend and contort the model like an '80s era toy, rather than taking it apart and reassembling it from scratch. It's an impressive feature.

The LEGO designers has been building towards a set of this size, scope, and ambition for some time. And now that they're finally here, it's something to behold – a homage to a Van Gogh painting that does its inspiration justice.

The designers worked alongside the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam, which is evident from their meticulous attention to detail. From its errant leaves and stems to its yellow-on-yellow-on-yellow color palette, this set is a piece of pop art that will look beautiful on any wall. We reviewed this set and can attest to its three-dimensional beauty.

This massive build of the Elves' ancestral home comes in three parts: an Elven tower that contains Bilbo's quarters, the bridge over the River Brunein, and the House of Elrond, including the council area where Frodo presented the one true ring. Everything, owing to its delicate structure, looks light and slightly unreal.

This LEGO Lord of the Rings set contains 15 Minifigures, including everyone in the Fellowship and every major character in Rivendell: Gandalf, Legolas, Gimli, Aragorn, Boromir, Frodo, Sam, Merry, Pippin, Gloin, Arwen, Elrond, Bilbo, and two elves. Check out our LEGO Rivendell review , as well as our interview with the designer .

Jurassic World Dinosaur Fossils: Tyrannosaurus rex

This set is better than its Jurassic World corporate branding might indicate. This is not some fanciful, Hollywood depiction of history's most famous dinosaur; the designers took pains to make it as accurate as it is imposing. Its barrel-like body, which hangs low to the ground, reflects our modern understanding of the T-rex, which we once believed to walk more upright. It's approximately 3.5 feet long – a 1:12 scale model of the real thing.

This massive set of Jabba's sail barge, made famous by Star Wars Episode VI: Return of the Jedi, is the best of what LEGO can dream up and design . It nails the exterior presentation, but its interior is even more impressive. Its top deck detaches and its sides flip up to reveal a cockpit, a prison, a kitchen, and a main throne room. It comes with 11 minifigures, including a massive Jabba figuirine, Salacious Crumb, Max Rebo, and Leia in her slave regalia.

A huge undertaking, the Venusaur, Charizard and Blastoise set is three separate builds – one of each Pokémon in its respective biome – which you can merge together to create a beautiful, massive centerpiece. The color variety in this set makes it eye-catching and fun, even from a distance. We built this set for its launch , and we were impressed by both its design and its engaging build process.

The newest entry on our 'Best LEGO Sets' list, Minas Tririth is a formidable accomplishment – a rich, rewarding build that deserves to be savored over a number of weeks, rather than rushed through in a couple of sittings. You build multiple layers and floors to this build, starting with the Great Gate that surrounds the city and working up to the Citadel and the Court of the Fountain at the very top. And just like the other sets, the end result matches the effort you put into building it. We did a full review and gallery of this build if you'd like to check it out.

The Modular Buildings are the original LEGO adult builds. The line began in 2007 and has since grown to include 21 sets – each a closed building on all four sides, and each connectable to the others with a common sidewalk base.

This set, the Tudor Corner, adds some Old World charm with its vintage architecture, and it includes a clockmaker's workshop, a haberdashery, and a sit-down restaurant on the bottom floor. It's eight minifigures include a chimney sweep and skilled craftsman with an epic, attachble moustache.

There are some LEGO sets that are magnificent looking, but have a tedious build process. There are other LEGO sets that have a fun, engaging build process, but are merely presentable without being exceptional.

And then there are the preferable LEGO sets, like these, which manage to be both – engaging and fun with little instructional redundancy, and an end result that looks every bit the effort and care placed into it.

If you found this list helpful, check out our other buying guides. We rounded up the Best LEGO Star Wars Sets , the Best Adult LEGO Sets the Best LEGO Alternatives , and the Best LEGO Marvel Sets as well.

Kevin Wong is a contributing freelancer for IGN, specializing in LEGO. He's also been published in Complex, Engadget, Gamespot, Kotaku, and more. Follow him on Twitter at @kevinjameswong .

articles.title: Brad Bird’s Ray Gunn Takes Viewers Back to the Future With This Fun Animated Love Letter to Film Noir and Retro Sci-Fi
articles.summary: Director Brad Bird’s Ray Gunn is a love letter to film noir and old-school science fiction, beautifully bringing its retro-futuristic world to life with great style and attention to detail.
articles.body:
Ray Gunn opens in select theaters on December 4 and arrives on Netflix on December 18. The film premiered on October 10 at the London Film Festival.

A 30-odd-year passion project for director Brad Bird, Ray Gunn is a nifty sci-fi/film noir mashup that’s sumptuously designed and cleverly realized, but is slightly dinged by an overlong runtime and occasionally clunky story.

Set in the vast futuristic city of Metropia, Ray Gunn follows its titular private eye (voiced by Sam Rockwell) as he and his one-eyed alien partner, Eye-Ra (Tom Waits), investigate a case involving the world’s biggest pop star, Venus Nova (Scarlett Johansson), that leads to murder, corruption and other nefarious things. If that sounds pretty gritty for an animated film from the director of The Incredibles and Ratatouille, it is.

Ray Gunn definitely leans toward a slightly older demographic than the broader audience of Bird’s past films for Pixar, which is perfectly fine since animation can obviously be more than just one kind of movie made specifically for children. While it may not be a zany animated comedy for the whole family, Ray Gunn still offers its share of cartoon hijinks for anyone who does watch it with their kids. Ray’s particle blaster pistol yields some raucous moments that would otherwise be considered body horror in a more serious film, and there’s a little alien version of essentially a French bulldog that satisfies the cute factor.

The alien designs are rather familiar but appropriate for the world these characters inhabit. The film uses some of these alien designs for humor and utility, such as Eye-Ra’s spider-like climbing skills. Other aliens are homages to film noir characters. The Jabba-like crime lord Slugsy is clearly patterned after The Maltese Falcon and Casablanca actor Sydney Greenstreet while his little henchman looks and sounds just like Peter Lorre.

The aliens who inhabit Metropia also serve as the film’s metaphor for a world where segregation and xenophobia still exist but are applied to aliens instead of humans. Aliens do all the manual labor and are banned from entering certain human facilities (for example, aliens must go to their own hospitals). There were even more avenues Ray Gunn could’ve taken to explore these serious issues a bit deeper. Unfortunately, the most noteworthy discussion about how the film explores its metaphor for racism can’t be discussed here due to major spoilers, but it was something different than an animated movie has broached before and the film handles it thoughtfully.

Ray Gunn drags a bit in the middle as the story winds its ways through the requisite beats of a detective procedural, trying to misdirect the viewer on things and characters that seemed rather obvious all along. The film, especially during its homestretch, also packs in a lot of under-explored messaging about the entertainment industry, technology and human nature without delving deeply enough to explore any of those topics beyond the cursory.

On a technical level, Ray Gunn boasts a stellar retro-futuristic aesthetic across the board, from its architecture to its costumes and gizmos and vehicles. This is a beautiful looking and sounding film (one that was especially enjoyable in a Dolby theater, so it’s a shame that most people probably won’t discover Ray Gunn until it lands on Netflix).

Ray Gunn: Brad Bird's Next Animated Film

Composer Michael Giacchino’s moody score sounds exactly like one you’d hear in a 1940s movie, especially during more dialogue-driven or romantic scenes. All of the creative elements make Ray Gunn pulpy fun with an old-school sci-fi gloss.

The voice cast are uniformly solid across the board, with Rockwell leading the pack as the hardboiled but glib gumshoe who somehow holds on to his optimism. The cynicism that’s inherent in film noir is provided here by Eye-Ra, who Waits plays with just the right mix of world-weariness and wry wit. Matt Berry is suitably erudite but sleazy as the voice of Slugsy, while Bobby Canavale, Alan Tudyk, Michelle Rodriguez and Kether Donohue all get their respective moments to shine in supporting roles.

And it should come as no surprise that Scarlett Johansson lends a breathy sultriness to the film’s femme fatale Venus Nova, but what might surprise you is how fine of a singer she is. Composer Kimbra provides three songs for the film that Johansson performs, with “Innocent” being the biggest earworm of the group.

articles.title: Star Citizen Single-Player Spinoff Squadron 42 Reemerges With Flashy New Trailer, Steam Wishlists, and Cast Confirmation
articles.summary: Star Citizen developer Cloud Imperium Games has pulled back the curtain on single-player spinoff Squadron 42 with a new cinematic trailer, the launch of Steam wishlists, and a full cast reveal.
articles.body:
Star Citizen developer Cloud Imperium Games has pulled back the curtain on single-player spinoff Squadron 42 with a new cinematic trailer, the launch of Steam wishlists, and a full cast reveal.

Squadron 42 is the story-driven off-shoot of space sim Star Citizen, which Cloud Imperium Games has worked on for the last 12 years. Its 12-year development is led by Chris Roberts, creator of the Wing Commander series. Indeed, Squadron 42 is a spiritual successor to Wing Commander, and like the Wing Commander games, Squadron 42 features a string of Hollywood stars, such as Mark Hamill, Gary Oldman, Gillian Anderson, Ben Mendelsohn, and Henry Cavill.

The game fuses space combat, first-person shooter action, and a character-driven narrative supported by full performance capture. CIG said the performances are woven directly into gameplay, so you won’t just see those famous actors within cinematics.

The year is 2945, and the United Empire of Earth stands on the verge of collapse as threats from outlaws and hostile alien forces emerge from the darkest reaches of space. Players enlist as a rookie in the UEE Navy, embarking on a dangerous journey that will take them from a recruit to the heart of a galactic war. Stationed aboard a massive capital ship, they’ll live and work alongside a dynamic crew, forge relationships, and face the sacrifices and split-second decisions that will shape their path forward as they earn their place, their rank, and their legacy.

And here’s what to expect from the structure of the game:

Whether maneuvering through a space battle, stealthily moving through an enemy-held location, or making a critical decision alongside fellow crew members, players will experience the story firsthand through a mix of action, exploration, and interactive cinematic sequences. Together, these elements pair the scale of a space epic with the personal stakes of a story about the people fighting to survive it.

The trailer shows a decent amount of gameplay, including first-person sections, some of which involve platforming and puzzle solving, ship customization, off duty activities, a hacking mini-game, and a glimpse at narrative choices. Ian Duncan, best known for playing Todd Todmore on BBC comedy Broken News, is the male player character, and prolific video game actor Alix Wilton Regan (Samantha Traynor in Mass Effect 3, the female Inquisitor in Dragon Age: Inquisition, Aya in Assassin's Creed Origins, and Lara Croft in the upcoming Tomb Raider games) plays the female player character.

In August, CIG delayed Squadron 42 to Q2 2027 , with Roberts insisting it wouldn’t get the attention it deserves if it came out at the end of 2026 because of November’s GTA 6.

"At CitizenCon 2024, we announced we would ship in 2026. Our plan was to release in Q4 around IAE," Roberts said at the time. "But much like the rest of the industry there is no way I want to launch my spiritual successor to Wing Commander, a game that has had 12 years of blood, sweat and tears invested into it (we started Squadron 42 development in 2014 as 2013 was opening studios, hiring people and getting the Hangar module out for Star Citizen) launching into the attention buzz saw of GTA 6. While GTA 6 isn’t launching on PC this November, pretty much all outlets and most content creators will be all over it, not leaving a lot of room for other coverage."

The delay announcement came hot on the heels of a disastrous Star Citizen developer livestream that went radically off the rails . After early access players complained of bugs and issues with a new update to the game, CIG held a stream to show the "intended" version of the experience, only to be met with the same issues, if not worse. It led to passive-aggressive comments between the developers themselves and an uncomfortable tension in the air.

Star Citizen crossed the $1 billion raised barrier in May — a significant milestone that came shortly after a $5,000 virtual spaceship you couldn’t actually fly in-game went on sale. It’s since raised a further $50 million.

Star Citizen is considered one of the most controversial projects in all video games. Over the 14 years since its crowdfunding drive began, Star Citizen has been called many things, including a scam by those who wonder whether it will ever properly launch. Its virtual ships, some of which cost thousands of dollars, are often the focus of criticism. But its loyal fanbase insist it's one of the most compelling space sims around, and continue to pump millions of dollars into the project via ship sales.

Star Citizen itself remains without a release window.

Wesley is IGN's Managing Editor. Find him on Twitter at @wyp100. You can reach Wesley at wesley_yinpoole@ign.com or confidentially at wyp100@proton.me.

articles.title: Hands-on Impressions of Hoid's Storybook Collection by Brandon Sanderson
articles.body:
Cosmere fans rejoice! The latest Brandon Sanderson Cosmere book , as a part of Hoid’s Storybook Collection, has started arriving for BackerKit backers. I had backed at the Storyteller tier when the campaign first launched and received my ebooks, PDFs, and audiobook all at once on Sept. 15. Then on Oct. 5 I received my physical books, stickers, pins, and more.

Here are my initial impressions on the latest BackerKit campaign from Dragonsteel.

The Fires of December Premium Book, eBook, and Audiobook

The Fires of December is the third book in what Sanderson is calling Hoid’s Travails. Fans of Tress of the Emerald Sea and Yumi and the Nightmare Painter (the other two stories in Hoid’s Travails) will want to get their hands on December right away. It is a standalone Cosmere book in a sense. December, the protagonist, is on a new planet in the Cosmere with her own plot and storyline. Where it connects to the Tress and Yumi is the narrator of the book is everyone’s favorite Worldhopper, Hoid.

The presentation of the premium hardcover book is stunning. The cover features custom art with gold trim that is much prettier in person than it was in pictures. Backers will remember that there were two options for the cover art for December. I went with the close-up one, and am really happy with how it turned out. The book also contains colored text and beautiful illustrations throughout. Artist Tran Nguyen did an excellent job of bringing the story to life. The way the golds, reds, blues, and purples work together to make this world leap off the page is very well done, making this book a worthy addition to any Sandershelf collection.

I have only read the first handful of chapters so far, but my initial impression has me hooked. The first chapter of the book reminded me of one of my favorite PS5 games, Returnal. I won’t say more to avoid spoilers, but you can listen to the first few chapters on Sanderson’s YouTube channel if you want to see for yourself.

If you didn’t get a chance to join the BackerKit, you can still get the standard edition ebook, audiobook, and physical book (though not the premium hardcovers). The digital versions became available on October 6 and the physical edition will be released on December 8, 2026.

The Fires of December: A Cosmere Novel (Hoid's Travails)

Hoid’s Storybook Collection Picture Books

For fans of the Stormlight Archive, it has long been clear that the chapters where Hoid tells stories to teach Kaladin and Shallan were a perfect fit for their own storybooks. To see these stories illustrated and published is a dream come true for me.

The Dog and the Dragon, The Girl Who Looked Up, and Wandersail are the three stories brought to our world from the pages of the Stormilight Archive. The fourth illustrated book in the collection, The ChasmFriends Get a Pet, is an original story written by Sanderson’s friend and podcast co-host Dan Wells.

The books themselves are illustrated by a few different talented artists. Howard Lyon did The Dog and the Dragon, Alexis and Justin Hernandez did The Girl Who Looked Up, Steve Argyle did Wandersail, and Anna Early on The Chasm Friends Get a Pet. Each book has its own unique style that feels like it fits the story that it is attached to. The art in The Dog and the Dragon and Chasm Friends is whimsical and playful, while the Wandersail and the Girl Who Looked Up are both epic fantasy illustrations worthy of the world of Roshar.

The story of The Dog and the Dragon in Rhythm of War is one of my favorite chapters I’ve read in any book. It's amazing to have a fully illustrated version I can share with my family and friends without making them read through thousands of pages of Stormlight first.

Overall, I’m happy with what I received in the Hoid’s Storybook Collection campaign. The premium hardcover of The Fires of December is truly a work of art worthy of any shelf. I can’t wait to dive into the full story, see all of the illustrations, and go on a journey with December to wherever her destination may lead to. The four picture books are exactly what Stormlight Archive fans have imagined them to be as well, and I am looking forward to sharing these stories with my children in the coming days. The artwork is amazing and the stories are each meaningful to me in their own ways.

articles.title: Blumhouse Gives Updates on Paranormal Activity 8, Saw 11, River, Something Is Killing the Children, and More | NYCC 2026
articles.summary: Friday night at New York Comic Con was all about Blumhouse, with a 90 minute "Blumfest" panel that was devoted to a ton of upcoming films from the combined forces of Jason Blum's Blumhouse and James Wan's Atomic Monster.
articles.body:
Friday night at New York Comic Con was all about Blumhouse, with a 90 minute "Blumfest" panel that was devoted to a ton of upcoming films from the combined forces of Jason Blum's Blumhouse and James Wan's Atomic Monster.

The panel kicked off with the reveal that moderator and YouTuber MatPat had signed a deal with Blumhouse to produce films based on indie horror games, along with announcement that their first project would be Amanda the Adventurer: The Movie . From there, MatPat, Blumhouse founder Jason Blum, and Atomic Monster founder James Wan went on to preview a ton of other projects to varying degrees, from quick status checks, to director announcements, to trailer debuts and cast appearances.

Director Mike Flanagan and cast member Chiwetel Ejiofor were on hand for the debut of the trailer for the upcoming new entry in The Exorcist franchise. Flanagan noted he had set a goal for himself to make Martyrs the scariest project he'd ever made and said he thinks he's succeeded, declaring, "This movie is so goddamn scary. I could feel it on set. I can’t wait for you guys to see it."

You can get a lot more insight from Flanagan about The Exorcist: Martyrs and what is glimpsed in the trailer — including the notable influence of The Exorcist III — in IGN's exclusive new Q&A with the filmmaker .

Known for her horror reviews and horror movie scene recreations, content creator Heidi Wong, AKA the Horror Queen, made an appearance to announce she will be writing and directing an original short film for Blumhouse. Blum the plan is to then develop the concept to hopefully make into a feature film as well.

Wong didn't want to give plot specifics yet but said that her story is inspired by Eastern mythology and folklore and that having grown up in Asia, it was subject matter she was close to.

A recent sensation at TIFF, where it premiered, this slasher movie became part of a bidding war before Universal, in partnership with Blumhouse and Atomic Monster won out, paying $10 million for distribution.

A trailer was shown for the film, which hasn't been officially released wide yet (but there might be some "filmed from the screen" versions out there) and it was highly effective and freaky, as Jessica Rothe's character goes swimming in a river, only for a hulking, silent man (Dane DiLiegro) leaps in the water and swims straight at her, quickly threatening to catch up to her as she desperately tries to make it back to the boat holding her siblings (Jane Levy and Max Mattern).

Rothe was there to promote the film, and the Happy Death Day star called River "a wild fucking ride, guys!"

Quick check ins were done for several franchise reboots on the way from Blumhouse and Atomic Monster, though there was not a lot of actual new info for the likes of RoboCop (this time a Prime Video series) and the next entries in the Blair Witch and Saw entries, beyond reiterating previously revealed factors, like Dan Stevens starring in RoboCop and Dylan Clark directing the fourth Blair Witch Project film.

But there was a bit more of a coy non-reveal for Saw 11, with Blum saying how important it was to purchase the franchise and put it back under the guidance of Wan and Leigh Whannell, who made the original film together. Blum promised they'd bring Saw back "in a whole new way," while Wan said he chose Mike P. Nelson to direct because he felt like he was a good fit as a filmmaker, including a talent for delivering surprises.

Asked what he felt was the most essential element to making a Saw movie, Wan implied there was a crucial part of the movie he had to keep a secret still, saying, "The thing that I really want to say, I cannot say just yet. What makes a Saw movie a Saw movie, I think you guys just have to wait... it'll be worth it!"

Blumhouse got its start with the original Paranormal Activity and Blum said while that would always mean the title was very significant to him, it was actually Wan who pushed to make a new one.

Wan said he felt they could "make a movie as scary as the first one and really pay tribute to the first one." And as it turns out, that will include quite literally returning to the first film's events in some capacity. A video from set had director Ian Tuason say they would be "taking you back to a familiar space," as footage from the original film was intercut to make sure we realized the set Tuason was standing on was the bedroom from the first Paranormal Activity that belonged to the ill-fated Katie and Micah.

Molepeople announced, starring Lakeith Stanfield

Director Rob Savage was on hand both to promote the film he has hitting theaters this weekend, Other Mommy , but he and Wan also announced his next project, Molepeople.

Savage described Molepeople as "a subturanan horror movie that's gonna scare the living shit out of you. It's in the vein of The Texas Chainsaw Massacre and The Hills Have Eyes. "

Savage revealed Lakeith Stanfield will star. Stanfield made a surprise appearance, saying he was drawn to the film because he found it to be "something I thought can be engaging, action packed, cool, fun, and then also a little bit of commentary too; something to think about."

Obsession writer-director Curry Barker and one of that film's stars, Cooper Tomlinson, were there to talk about their new film, the comedy-horror Anything But Ghosts, along with reflecting on Obsession's amazing box office success and how it's changed their lives since it opened.

Anything But Ghosts stars Barker and Tomlinson as two "ghost hunter con artists," who put on a big show to mask their trickery, and what happens when they get the biggest job they've ever had, only to need to figure out what to do when this turns out to be the real thing in the ghost department. The film recently got a release date for May 7, 2027.

Barker and Tomlinson had made and starred in comedy shorts together for years before Obsession, but Barker ended up not having an on-camera role in Obsession. When it came Anything But Ghosts, though, the duo noted they always imagined they'd star in it from the time it was being written. Blum had high praise for Barker in the movie, saying he couldn't imagine anyone else in the role now that he's seen it.

Something is Killing the Children has a director

The night wrapped up with the announcement that Blumhouse's adaptation of the comic book Something is Killing the Children has found its director: Craig Zobel (The Hunt, The Penguin).

The comics' co-creator, writer James Tynion IV, said he and artist/co-creator Werther Dell'Edera "always knew this was a franchise with the potential to meet a much, much bigger audience," which they felt the film version would allow them to realize.

The next key component will be casting the lead character, Erica Slaughter, in this story of a mother hunting down monsters that target kids. Tynion spoke about Erica's considerable strength, both mental and physical, while also noting how funny she can be, something he thinks should be an important part of the casting process.

And rest assured, Octo the octopus toy was promised to be in the film...

articles.title: GTA 6 Leaker Threatens to Release Build With Full Story Mode Played to the End, Ties Lucia's Clothing to Crypto Scheme
articles.summary: The GTA 6 leaker has reportedly threatened to release a build of the game with the full story mode played to the end, as part of their heavily criticized crypto scheme.
articles.body:
The GTA 6 leaker has reportedly threatened to release a build of the game with the full story mode played to the end, as part of their heavily criticized crypto scheme.

According to online reports , the Cyberleek website was updated with a warning that if its memecoin reached a market cap of $30 million, a build of GTA 6 would be released featuring the full story mode including end credits. In the alleged online warning, Cyberleek once again framed their GTA 6 leaks as a protest against the lack of a physical disc version of the game, and allegedly called on Take-Two to release GTA 6 on-disc and issue an apology. It is unclear whether Cyberleek intends to release a build of the game online, or means to release a full playthrough of GTA 6 in video form.

A cryptocurrency market capitalization (market cap) is the total dollar value of all the coins or tokens of a digital asset currently in circulation. At the time of this article’s publication, Cyberleek had a market cap of $3.8 million, having spiked at $5.7 million earlier today as reports of the message hit social media. It seems unlikely that it will get anywhere near $30 million.

In Pictures: How GTA 6's Jason and Lucia Have Evolved Since 2023

Here's the deal, nice and clean. CYBERLEEK hits 30 million marketcap, the build goes out — full story mode, played to the end, credits and all. Don't believe it has full story mode? Ask for what you want to see, and it gets provided. Take-Two gets one way out: physical disks and a public apology. They can take it at any moment. Or they can gamble that CL is bluffing. Everyone knows which one they'll pick.

Cyberleek also issued market cap goals tied to the clothing Lucia would wear in subsequent leaked gameplay. For example, at $2 million, Cyberleek threatened to release gameplay showing Lucia wearing a bikini. According to Cyberleek, a $4 million market cap would mean releasing gameplay with Lucia “fully naked.”

However, there is significant skepticism about Cyberleek’s support of physical media, with many accusing the leaker of running a cryptocurrency scam. Fans have heavily criticized Cyberleek and anyone who spends money on their memecoin. “What a dork,” one person said. “Anyone who puts money into this deserves to lose it all.”

Cyberleek appeared to go dark after a spate of high-profile GTA 6 leaks in August that sparked an investigation from Rockstar parent company Take-Two. The film issued subpoenas to the likes of Discord as part of the hunt for the person or group of people responsible. But Cyberleek reemerged this week with the release of a 24-minute GTA 6 gameplay video that showed cutscenes, story beats, playable characters Jason and Lucia naked (in the case of Jason, full-frontal nudity), and a first-person camera.

It remains unclear how the gameplay footage, or any potential build of the game it's taken from, escaped the confines of Rockstar's infamous tight security. This week’s developments suggest Cyberleek remains at large and defiant in the face of potential legal action.

In August, Rockstar addressed the GTA 6 leaks , describing the situation as "heartbreaking" for its development team and "unfortunate" for fans. At the time, the developer acknowledged that its intended experience for players "may now be impacted by some spoilers," but reiterated GTA 6's previously-confirmed launch date of November 19.

Analysis of cryptocurrency transactions in late August pointed to the GTA 6 leaker having "cashed out," earning around $270,000 in the process. Every video posted by Cyberleek pointed to a website where fans could pay to vote on further leaks using the leaker's own cryptocurrency. Such a poll is reportedly live on Cyberleek's website now , suggesting yet another leak is on the way.

articles.title: Nicolas Cage Says He'll 'Probably Never Work With' Amazon Again After Declining Spider-Noir AI Waiver
articles.summary: Nicolas Cage said he'll "probably never work with" Amazon again after declining to sign a waiver to use AI on Spider-Noir.
articles.body:
Nicolas Cage said he'll "probably not work with" Amazon again after declining to sign a waiver to use AI on Spider-Noir .

The National Treasure actor made his position on the controversial technology clear during a New York Comic Con 2026 panel attended by IGN. His work on Amazon's Prime Video Spider-Noir show officially came to an end when the Marvel project was canceled last month, but it doesn't sound like he would have been too excited to return for a second season anyway.

"Amazon is a very AI-friendly company, to the tune of $50 billion invested in OpenAI . I'm not an AI-friendly actor," Cage said. "I'm not part of their club. I didn't sign the waiver to use AI on Spider-Noir. I'll probably not work with that studio again, but that's OK."

Cage is far from a newcomer to the growing list of Hollywood talent to come out against AI in recent years. In early 2025, the actor used the Saturn Awards as an opportunity to speak against artificial intelligence, saying he's "a big believer in not letting robots dream for us."

"Robots cannot reflect the human condition for us," he continued. "That is a dead end if an actor lets one AI robot manipulate his or her performance even a little bit, an inch will eventually become a mile and all integrity, purity, and truth of art will be replaced by financial interests only. We can’t let that happen."

He also told The New Yorker that he was "terrified" of AI in 2024. Now that Cage is likely writing off working with Amazon, it sounds like he's putting his money where his mouth is.

Cage isn't just avoiding AI; he's also backing other anti-AI filmmakers. One fresh face in the Hollywood scene that he had kind words for at NYCC was YouTuber-turned-director Kane Parsons. The budding moviemaker behind Backrooms previously called attention to the " genuinely harmful consequences " generative AI has inflicted on society, and now, Cage just so happens to be a fan.

"I got to get with these young directors who are, you know, Gen Z, and they're going in it their own way, whether it's through the YouTube culture or whatever it is," the actor said. "They're doing it from scratch by hand. I wanna get with that."

The Face/Off star's time in the live-action Spider-Noir may have come to an end, but it won't be long before we see him on our screens again. Cage is attached to star in Madden as John Madden in what may be his final project with Amazon MGM. He's also expected to appear in the next season of True Detective , and he'll lend his voice chops to the Marvel universe once again when he shows up for Spider-Man: Beyond the Spider-Verse in 2027.

Cage commented on Spider-Noir's cancellation shortly after the news broke: "For me, one season is perfect, having said what I wanted to say with this dangerous, innovative, pop-art Spider-Man. Onwards, upwards, inwards."

Photo by Michael Loccisano/Getty Images.

articles.title: DC Legend Grant Morrison Criticizes 'Morally and Legally Incoherent' Lanterns Finale
articles.summary: DC veteran Grant Morrison reviewed Lanterns, and they had more than a few criticisms of its "morally and legally incoherent" finale.
articles.body:
DC veteran Grant Morrison reviewed Lanterns , and they had more than a few criticisms of its "morally and legally incoherent" finale.

The comic book writer – who worked on projects like The Green Lantern, Doom Patrol, and many more – made their feelings about the new DCU TV show clear in a new post for their Xanaduum Substack . Overall, they said, Lanterns "worked," but their thoughts on the package as a whole are a bit complicated.

Morrison admitted they "fell asleep" while watching Lanterns episodes 6 and 7. That's "not because they were boring," though; it's just that watching TV "feels like a much-appreciated moment of relaxation and drift." For them, the Green Lantern HBO series actually managed to mostly pull off its True Detective-inspired story, and that's thanks to two things: Aaron Pierre's John Stewart and Kyle Chandler's Hal Jordan .

"Lanterns worked as a show and it’s mostly down to the two leads, particularly Kyle Chandler as Hal Jordan," Morrison explained. "They have a great supporting cast which helps, but it’s the two principals and their chemistry and charisma that sells the whole thing – so maybe those True Detective comparisons had some basis after all!"

Warning! Spoilers for the Lanterns Season 1 finale follow.

It's a mostly glowing start to their review that quickly took a turn for the worse. The DC legend then said they "didn't really like the ending," even if it was all "neatly put together." Their primary issue lies with Kelly Macdonald's Sheriff Kerry, who split the fanbase when she was revealed to be Hal Jordan's killer in the show's final moments.

The actual moment itself is quite tense, showing the character firing a single shot at the Green Lantern hero after he discovered her son, Noah, was a Manhunter in disguise. He's only able to give out half of a game plan and a quick "I love you" before his time in the DCU was cut short, and it's led many to raise complaints about how it all played out. For Morrison, it was hard to accept that "everyone seemed fine with that psychotic break."

"There should probably have been some response to that, because otherwise it makes it really hard for the audience to work out what makes the Green Lantern Corps an intergalactic law enforcement agency at all," they said. "The Guardians are now fine with their operatives being murdered while other officers simply ignore the fact and let the perps walk free?"

The Green Lantern writer then acknowledged and explanation from Lanterns writer and fellow comic book author Tom King. King said Kerry's having to live with her actions was punishment enough, but that's not a satisfying enough answer for Morrison.

"I watched the show; Kerry lost her shit in a way that made her seem unhinged and she shot a superhero in the head out of pique," they added. "John Stewart also let the Manhunter go free, knowing that he could one day destroy the world. For a show that’s not about masked vigilantes with their own personal code but deals with weird space policemen working for an interplanetary judiciary, it was a morally and legally incoherent conclusion that backed out of its own implications and the basic premise of the franchise."

Although there are rumors of a Lanterns Season 2 being in early development at HBO, Morrison isn't holding their breath for things to pan out. Although there have been some teases – particularly from bad guy Sinestro (Ulrich Thomsen) – about bringing back Chandler as Parallax, losing Hal Jordan could mean losing half of what made the show so great for many. Pierre is great, but without that dynamic, there's no telling how a second season could land the plane like the first. As Morrison said, "We'll see."

Meanwhile, Morrison is continuing their work in the comic book world with a new project outside of the DC wheelhouse. As announced at New York Comic Con 2026, the author is now set to work with IDW Publishing on a new run based on James Bond . Details about how it fits into the 007 universe have yet to be revealed.
